Government should change course in several places. First, several Secure steps get little recorded attention. Uranium conversion and enrichment, rare-earth and battery-metal refining and gas production rank low among South Korea's own policy priorities (
out of a hundred). Battery materials refining, a Catch Up step, sits below the middle (

out of a hundred). Second, deployment policy lags for solar and wind. Finally, protection runs ahead of the case in grid components, where the strategy is to partner, and in oil refining, gas liquids processing, wafers and PV cells and grid networks.

sections.title: Strategic agenda — what should South Korea do next?

blocks.text: 1. Secure fuels and nuclear fuel through trusted contracts and stocks

inlines.v: Hold fuel stocks sized to the rebuild time, with long-term and capacity-reservation contracts across trusted producers. Supply the national-security end uses of uranium conversion and enrichment from trusted sources only, while the civilian market stays open. Build trusted capacity with partners through long-term contracts, co-investment and shared stockpiles with trusted processors such as
Canada, the United Kingdom and France

blocks.text: 2. Secure the rare-earth chain with allied refiners

inlines.v: Build diversified, qualified supply with trusted refiners such as
the United States, Japan and Australia
through offtake, public finance and allied agreements, hold stockpiles until it qualifies, and invest in recycling. No developing partner qualifies at rare-earth and battery-metal refining;
, the step that holds the rare-earth separation layer.

blocks.text: 3. Keep the battery chain at the frontier and close the materials gap

inlines.v: Preserve cells and packs through next-generation research, workforce and supplier development, and finance for expansion tied to benchmarks. In battery components and materials, use time-limited production support, first-of-a-kind finance and demand creation, all tied to benchmarks, and keep the gate open to joint ventures that transfer capability. This is where the national task and the allied role coincide.

Offer allies trusted battery materials and components, electric rail vehicles, transformers and gas plant through offtake and co-investment, and secure minerals in return through offtake and co-investment with
the United States, Canada and Australia
. Protection of grid components should give way to partnership terms.

blocks.text: 5. Build trusted battery and drivetrain capacity with developing partners

inlines.v: , where groundwork comes first. Also start with

, where Korean firms already invest. Use project preparation, standards and skills where the constraint is a public good, and development finance, guarantees and offtake where it is bankability. Move aid that still reaches commercial-route partners toward partners that need groundwork.

blocks.text: 6. Accelerate nuclear, solar and wind while keeping sourcing open

inlines.v: Close the deployment-policy gap for solar and wind, and keep nuclear and EV adoption on pace, through infrastructure, permitting and procurement. Buy turbines, modules and commodity hardware competitively from trusted suppliers, and attach trusted-supplier and security conditions to public deployment support and to equipment with built-in control.
Every number comes from the Country page data of the Allied Industrial Base Explorer (the data release of
) and from the Allied Industrial Base analysis. Each technology is split into supply-chain stages, from extraction to recycling, and each step gets a strategic choice by fixed rules applied in order:
Secure where an acute vulnerability is measured;
at deployment, Accelerate where deployment need reaches
Watch where the step is a large, commoditized yard;
Preserve where Competitive Position is in the top quarter (
Catch Up where the value is high, the position is not, and a capability anchor is corroborated by other evidence;
Partner where supply-chain need is high but there is neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway;

Named layers inside a step, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice, and a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed. A value that rests on market size alone is capped just under the bar. Observed policy never decides a choice. The high fence (Secure) protects what cannot be allowed to fail; the medium fence covers capabilities worth building, keeping or sourcing deliberately and deployment to accelerate; the low fence (Watch) leaves a step open to competitive purchase.

A pair joins a Korean step with a strategic reason for more allied capacity and a developing economy (not high income) whose same step is a Catch Up. The partner needs an anchor corroborated beyond context signals, sufficient evidence and confidence, and a place inside the AIB trust screen; on a step whose data describe different products, the anchor must measure the product the need is about. A partner that already hosts the step's new capacity in the AIB, or Preserves it, is a commercial case. Aid comes from the OECD Creditor Reporting System by purpose code. Components and Assembly share codes, no code funds recycling, and many codes name a stage rather than a technology, so aid at a step is not aid for that technology. Aid is called technology-coded only where codes naming the technology hold most of it. A constraint on a partner is named only where the data observe its input; otherwise the table says the data do not cover it. In the relationship table an observed zero is stated as nothing recorded, data that do not cover a pair are left out, and the direct investment position is economy-wide, not tied to the step. Export-credit finance is reported apart and never counted as aid, and direct investment uses the IMF positions (the partner's reports where South Korea reports none).
